hero.name: Yusuf
hero.who: a 38-year-old hardware shop owner in Hyderabad who chases stock tips on WhatsApp

story.b: Yusuf runs a hardware shop in Secunderabad, selling pipes, paint and screws. Every morning, before he lifts the shutter, he checks the stock tips group his cousin added him to. Someone always has a sure shot. Last year Yusuf bought four of them. Two went up a little, and two fell so hard he stopped checking. He has also started watching late-night videos about chart patterns, tracing lines on price graphs with his finger. His wife Rukhsana asks how much the shares have made overall. He honestly does not know. He only remembers the wins. Meanwhile his daughter's school fees rise every year, and he wonders whether he is investing or gambling.

ask.q: Yusuf is not sure whether he is investing or gambling. What should he do first?
o: Join a bigger, more popular tips group
Put more money into the next sure shot to win back his losses
Step back and honestly add up how all his tips and trades have done
ask.why: A bigger tips group is still guessing, and chasing losses is how small mistakes grow. Adding up every trade honestly, including the losses he forgot, shows Yusuf whether his method actually works. That clear picture is the first step to a calmer plan.

chapters.take: If you only remember your wins, you do not know your results.

story.b: Yusuf buys a cheap notebook from the stationery shop next door. For one month, every time the group posts a confident prediction, he writes it down with the date and the price. He does not buy anything. He just waits. At the end of the month, he sits behind his counter after closing time and checks each one. Some went up. Some went down. Some did nothing at all. If he had tossed a coin, he thinks, he might have done just as well. He also notices that by the time a tip reached the group, the price had often already jumped. Next morning, Ramesh, a plumber who buys pipes from him, leans on the counter with exciting news about a share.

ask.q: Ramesh swears a certain share will double next week. What is Yusuf's wisest response?
o: Treat it as a guess, since short-term price moves are mostly unpredictable
Buy quickly before everyone else hears about it
Buy a small amount, just in case Ramesh is right
ask.why: By the time a tip reaches a plumber's phone and then Yusuf's counter, any real news is usually already in the price. Rushing in is betting on a guess, and a just-in-case amount is still a bet. Treating confident predictions as guesses protects his money.

chapters.take: Nobody can reliably predict next week's prices, however sure they sound.

story.b: For six months Yusuf has paid for an online course on chart patterns. He has learned words like support, resistance and breakout, and he enjoys using them with his cousin. But when he writes down how he actually picks shares, the list is short. A tip from the group. A pattern that looked right. A feeling. He then adds up his trades from the notebook and his broker app, including brokerage, taxes and the course fee itself. The total makes him sit back on his stool. After all the costs, he is roughly where he started, a little behind. That evening an email arrives, offering to renew the course for another year at twelve thousand rupees.

ask.q: The chart course wants twelve thousand rupees for another year. How should Yusuf decide?
o: Renew it, because drawing lines feels scientific and smart
Check honestly whether his chart trades beat simply holding the market, after all costs
Upgrade to a costlier course with better patterns
ask.why: Feeling clever while drawing lines is not the same as earning more. A costlier course adds fees without any proof. Comparing his chart trades, after the course fee and charges, with simply holding the whole market shows Yusuf whether the method is really working for him.

chapters.take: Feeling clever is not the same as earning more. Count every cost.

story.b: Yusuf's nephew Imran, who works in a bank's accounts department, comes over for biryani on Sunday. Over the meal, Yusuf admits what his notebook showed. Imran does not laugh. He explains index funds, which simply own all the companies in a market index instead of trying to pick winners. Fees are very low, and nobody has to guess anything. Yusuf takes out the statement of a fund an agent sold him years ago and finds its yearly fee in small print. He compares it with a low-cost index fund on his phone. The difference looks tiny for one year. Then he multiplies it by twenty years and puts his spoon down. The next week, a bank executive calls with another fund to sell.

ask.q: The bank executive pushes a high-fee fund that did very well last year. What should Yusuf weigh?
o: Last year's winner will probably keep winning, so fees do not matter
Whichever fund the executive sounds most excited about
Fees cut into returns every year, and few funds beat a low-cost index fund over long periods
ask.why: Last year's star often fades, and an executive's excitement may reflect commission rather than fit. A yearly fee comes out whether the fund does well or not, and over many years it adds up. A low-cost index fund owns the whole market without Yusuf guessing who is lucky.

chapters.take: When you cannot pick the winner, own the whole race cheaply.

story.b: By winter, every second customer in Yusuf's shop is talking about land. A new road is planned on the edge of the city, and plots near it have shot up in price. A contractor buying cement tells him he has booked two. Yusuf's cousin calls three times, saying prices will double again and Yusuf will regret missing out. Even the tea boy has opinions about square yards. Yusuf feels the pull in his chest. His savings sit in a dull bank account while everyone else seems to be getting rich. He remembers his notebook and the predictions that went nowhere. He also remembers his father talking about a similar rush years ago, and the half-built colonies that followed.

ask.q: Everyone in the market is rushing to buy plots, and prices keep jumping. What should Yusuf ask himself?
o: Would I still buy this if nobody around me was talking about it?
How fast can I buy before prices rise even further?
How can I borrow more to buy two plots instead of one?
ask.why: When everyone is excited and prices keep jumping, it is easy to believe this time is different. Rushing in or borrowing more lets the crowd's mood decide for Yusuf. Asking whether he would buy with nobody talking about it separates real value from excitement.

chapters.take: When everyone is sure prices only go up, slow down and think.

story.b: In March, Yusuf's father retires from the electricity board and receives a lump sum. He has heard Yusuf talk about shares for two years, and now he wants to put the entire amount into the market. Yusuf feels a chill. He thinks about how different their lives are. He is thirty-eight, with twenty years before he needs his long-term savings, so he can sit through bad years. His father is sixty, needs a monthly income soon and has no salary to fall back on. For himself, Yusuf has already started a small monthly SIP into an index fund, after keeping six months of shop expenses aside in a fixed deposit. His father's money needs a different plan.

ask.q: Yusuf's newly retired father wants to put his whole lump sum into shares. What should Yusuf suggest?
o: Go ahead, since shares did well for some of his friends
Match the plan to his age and needs, keeping most of it in safer options
Split it equally between shares and land plots
ask.why: Someone in retirement has less time to sit through market falls and may need the money soon. A friend's success says nothing about his father's needs, and land plus shares adds risk, not safety. Matching the mix to age, goals and comfort with ups and downs fits better, and a trusted adviser can help with details.

chapters.take: The right mix depends on your age, your goals and how long you can wait.

story.b: A year later, Yusuf is still in the stock tips group, but he has muted it. Sometimes he reads the predictions the way he reads cricket gossip, just for fun. His monthly SIP goes out on the fifth, the same day he pays his paint supplier, and he checks it only every few months. The chart course is gone. He did not buy a plot, and prices near the new road have stopped rising, though nobody at the shop mentions that. His father's money sits mostly in safer deposits, with a small part in an index fund, chosen after a long talk with an adviser at the bank. Rukhsana asks how the shares are doing. Yusuf says boringly, and they both smile.

chapters.take: Simple, low-cost, patient investing feels boring. For most people, boring is the point.
